citation: Hengartner, M. O., and H. R. Horvitz. "C. elegans Cell Survival Gene ced-9 Encodes a Functional Homolog of the Mammalian Proto-oncogene bcl-2." Cell 76, no. 4 (1994): 665–76.

citation: Kvansakul, M., M. F. van Delft, E. F. Lee, J. M. Gulbis, W. D. Fairlie, D. C. S. Huang, and P. M. Colman. "A Structural Viral Mimic of Prosurvival Bcl-2: A Pivotal Role for Sequestering Proapoptotic Bax and Bak." Molecular Cell 25, no. 6 (2007): 933–42.
reason: Known case 2: Myxoma virus M11L against BCL-2. The crystal structure of M11L bound to a Bak BH3 peptide shows the Bcl-2 fold and the same groove that BCL-2 uses to hold Bax and Bak.

citation: Cameron, C. M., J. W. Barrett, M. Mann, A. Lucas, and G. McFadden. "Myxoma Virus M128L Is Expressed as a Cell Surface CD47-like Virulence Factor That Contributes to the Downregulation of Macrophage Activation in Vivo." Virology 337, no. 1 (2005): 55–67.
reason: Known case 3: Myxoma virus M128L against CD47. M128L sits on the surface of infected cells as a CD47-like protein, and rabbits infected with virus lacking it had milder disease and more activated macrophages.

citation: Löwe, J., and L. A. Amos. "Crystal Structure of the Bacterial Cell-Division Protein FtsZ." Nature 391, no. 6663 (1998): 203–6.
reason: Known case 4: FtsZ against alpha- and beta-tubulin. The crystal structure of FtsZ has the tubulin fold and the same GTP-binding site. A bacterial cell-division protein and a human cytoskeleton protein are one family.

citation: van den Ent, F., L. A. Amos, and J. Löwe. "Prokaryotic Origin of the Actin Cytoskeleton." Nature 413, no. 6851 (2001): 39–44.
reason: Known case 5: MreB against actin. The crystal structure of MreB has the actin fold, and MreB forms protein filaments with the same subunit spacing as an actin filament.

citation: Schumacher, M. A., R. F. Pearson, T. Møller, P. Valentin-Hansen, and R. G. Brennan. "Structures of the Pleiotropic Translational Regulator Hfq and an Hfq–RNA Complex: A Bacterial Sm-like Protein." The EMBO Journal 21, no. 13 (2002): 3546–56.

citation: Graham, S. C., M. W. Bahar, S. Cooray, R. A.-J. Chen, D. M. Whalen, N. G. A. Abrescia, D. Alderton, et al. "Vaccinia Virus Proteins A52 and B14 Share a Bcl-2-like Fold but Have Evolved to Inhibit NF-κB Rather Than Apoptosis." PLoS Pathogens 4, no. 8 (2008): e1000128.
reason: Known case 7: Vaccinia virus A52 and B14 against BCL-2. The crystal structures of A52 and B14 have the Bcl-2 fold but no groove for a BH3 peptide. Neither protein changes programmed cell death; both block NF-κB signalling. The case also covers P24772.

citation: Essuman, K., D. W. Summers, Y. Sasaki, X. Mao, A. K. Y. Yim, A. DiAntonio, and J. Milbrandt. "TIR Domain Proteins Are an Ancient Family of NAD-Consuming Enzymes." Current Biology 28, no. 3 (2018): 421–430.e4.
reason: Known case 8: A bacterial TIR-domain protein against a human TIR domain. Purified TirS cleaves NAD, and the full-length protein lowers NAD in human cells, which the catalytically dead E216A protein does not. The human TIR domains of the Toll-like receptors hold protein complexes together instead.

citation: Tal, M. C., P. S. Hansen, H. A. Ogasawara, Q. Feng, R. F. Volk, B. Lee, S. E. Casebeer, et al. "P66 Is a Bacterial Mimic of CD47 That Binds the Anti-phagocytic Receptor SIRPα and Facilitates Macrophage Evasion by Borrelia burgdorferi." bioRxiv preprint, April 30, 2024.
reason: Known case 9: P66 against CD47. P66 binds the human receptor SIRPα, the receptor CD47 binds, and Borrelia lacking P66 is taken up by macrophages more readily.

citation: Buchwald, G., A. Friebel, J. E. Galán, W.-D. Hardt, A. Wittinghofer, and K. Scheffzek. "Structural Basis for the Reversible Activation of a Rho Protein by the Bacterial Toxin SopE." The EMBO Journal 21, no. 13 (2002): 3286–95.

citation: Stebbins, C. E., and J. E. Galán. "Modulation of Host Signaling by a Bacterial Mimic: Structure of the Salmonella Effector SptP Bound to Rac1." Molecular Cell 6, no. 6 (2000): 1449–60.

citation: Chen, L., A. L. DeVries, and C. H. Cheng. "Convergent Evolution of Antifreeze Glycoproteins in Antarctic Notothenioid Fish and Arctic Cod." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America 94, no. 8 (1997): 3817–22.
reason: Known case 12: Antifreeze glycoprotein, Antarctic notothenioid against Arctic cod. Both fish make the same ice-binding glycoprotein from a repeat of the same three residues. The notothenioid gene came from a trypsinogen and the cod gene did not, and the two genes differ in their introns, spacers and codon use.

citation: Marazzi, I., J. S. Y. Ho, J. Kim, B. Manicassamy, S. Dewell, R. A. Albrecht, C. W. Seibert, et al. "Suppression of the Antiviral Response by an Influenza Histone Mimic." Nature 483, no. 7390 (2012): 428–33.
